To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the subjective estimation of mood is correlated with EEG characteristics.

1) subjective estimation of mood correlates with EEG spectral power, 2) these correlations differ according to the frequency band and localization, and 3) these differences can be explained in terms of the underlying neurobiological mechanisms of EEG spectral power.
the subjective mood estimation is co-varied with the EEG characteristics, and that the co-variation is specific for the frequency and localization of the spectral power parameters.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between mood and brain activity.
the problem of the relationship between subjective mood estimation and the brain activity.
the problem of how the brain processes information about the emotional state of an organism.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the subjective estimation of mood/activation is reflected in a complex way in the EEG spectral power parameters, with different EEG parameters co-variating with different mood dimensions.
subjective estimation of mood/activation has a complex and specific co-variation with EEG spectral power parameters.
mood, in the sense of a subjective feeling, is not a single entity but a complex construct that can be described in terms of several different components, each of which has its own brain correlates.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the brain activity in the theta1, theta2 and beta1 bands is associated with the Tension-Calm dimension, and that the alpha1 band activity is associated with the Energy-Tiredness dimension.
EEG spectral power characteristics co-vary with subjectively estimated mood, but that the EEG correlates for the two mood dimensions differ.
subjective mood estimation has a specific EEG correlate.
The main takeaway from our work is that
mood estimation is not a simple, one-dimensional phenomenon.
the EEG correlates of mood estimation are not limited to a specific frequency band, and that the EEG correlates are not identical across the two dimensions of the ADACL.
the EEG correlates of mood can be described in terms of the frequency bands and their power, and not only by the topographical distribution of EEG activity.
